What is the OTIF threshold in our Master Logistics Agreement and what happens when a carrier breaches it?

The Master Logistics Agreement (MLA) 2023 sets the OTIF target at 95% across all contracted lanes. When a carrier falls below this threshold, a performance credit of 1.5% of monthly freight spend applies for each percentage point below 95%. The carrier must also submit a Service Improvement Plan (SIP) within 14 days of the breach. Repeated underperformance — three consecutive months below 90% — triggers a termination-for-cause clause. Currently FastFreight UK (88.3%), Nordic Express (91.2%), and TranzCargo Iberia (89.7%) are all in breach, with an estimated monthly credit run-rate of £287K annualised.

Which of our suppliers carry the most single-source risk and what is the mitigation strategy for each?

Our top three single-source risk suppliers are: (1) SemiCore for IC substrates at 23% production exposure — the primary risk is geopolitical disruption from Taiwan Strait tensions with a 16-week lead time. Mitigation is a dual-source programme with Kyocera (Japan), expected to complete qualification in Q4 2024. (2) Nexus Plastics for injection-moulded housings at 19% exposure — risk is a catastrophic event at their single Coventry facility. We have issued an RFQ to Plastiform SA in France with qualification expected Q3 2024. (3) FlexSeal GmbH for industrial seals at 17% exposure — the risk is key person dependency on a single formulation chemist. Mitigation is a technology transfer negotiation with Trelleborg AB currently underway. In parallel, safety stock policy has been amended to a minimum 12-week cover for all Category A suppliers, up from the previous 4-week policy.

What is the total financial impact of the US 25% tariff on Chinese electronics and how are we mitigating it?

The 25% US tariff on HTS Codes 8541-8543 (electronic components), effective 1 August 2024, impacts 22 NGO SKU families across Consumer Electronics Assembly and Smart Home Devices with a combined £26M annual procurement spend. The gross annual cost increase is £6.5M. For Q3 specifically the incremental cost is £4.2M. We are mitigating through Vietnam re-sourcing: Vinatex Electronics and HCM Components Ltd are both qualified suppliers capable of onboarding within 6–8 weeks, delivering an estimated £2.1M cost saving in Year 1. Category Manager Patricia Lim authorised an emergency PO to Vinatex for £3.1M of Q3 volumes on 15 July. The net FY2025 exposure after mitigation is £2.8M. Monterrey Industrial in Mexico is also an option and qualifies for USMCA 0% tariff treatment, but requires a 3-week vendor audit first.

Walk me through the Rotterdam port strike contingency plan for pharmaceutical SKUs.

Our Rotterdam port strike contingency plan prioritises pharmaceutical cold-chain SKUs (Priority A designation) given their regulatory and patient safety implications. The primary re-route redirects 68% of total Rotterdam volume to Hamburg (Germany) and Felixstowe (UK). Pharmaceutical cold-chain SKUs specifically are rerouted via the Antwerp air-freight corridor, with an incremental cost of £1.8M for a 3-week disruption window. Ambient SKUs shift to Hamburg rail connectors. We estimate full network recovery within 19 days. All seven 3PL partners have been notified with revised SLAs and rate schedules. The plan activates automatically when Rotterdam capacity drops below 40% of normal throughput, as monitored by our Lloyd's Intelligence port feed.

What does our Q4 demand forecast show for SKU FMCG-HPC-022 and what supply actions are needed?

The Q4 demand forecast for SKU FMCG-HPC-022 shows significant seasonal variability: July 1.2M units (baseline), August 1.4M units (+17% back-to-school uplift), September 1.9M units (+58% peak driven by the 6-week promotional campaign launching 1 September), October 1.1M units (post-promotional trough), November 1.6M units (Q4 seasonal ramp). The critical supply action is pre-building inventory: we recommend producing 800K units in June and July to buffer against the September demand spike. The DC-Birmingham warehouse has been flagged as a capacity constraint for the September peak — a 4,000 pallet temporary overflow arrangement with external storage provider StorBase has been proposed and is pending CPO approval. The forecast assumes 4.5% promotional uplift above historical September baselines based on the confirmed media spend plan.

What working capital savings can we achieve by implementing the inventory optimisation model recommendations?

Implementing the (s,S) replenishment policy with demand-sensing inputs across our 12 highest-velocity SKUs is projected to deliver a 21.4% working capital reduction — exceeding the 18% target. This is achieved by reducing reorder points by 8–23% per SKU through improved forecast accuracy, and recalculating safety stock using a Poisson demand model calibrated to a 99.2% fill rate. The implementation is phased: 4 SKUs in Month 1 (those with low forecast volatility and fast replenishment cycles — quick wins), the remaining 8 SKUs in Months 2 and 3. At current working capital of £87M tied up in safety stock for these SKUs, a 21.4% reduction represents approximately £18.6M in freed cash. The model is also designed to trigger automatic purchase orders when inventory hits the reorder point, removing the current 2–3 day manual cycle.

What are the key KPIs in the supply chain programme business case?

The Supply Chain Intelligence Programme business case centres on five financial KPIs: (1) Disruption cost reduction — a target 60% reduction in reactive disruption events, saving an estimated £20M against the 2022-2023 baseline of £34M in disruption costs. (2) Safety stock optimisation — 18% working capital reduction through demand-sensing and (s,S) replenishment, delivering £15.6M benefit against the £87M excess safety stock baseline. (3) 3PL performance improvement — contract enforcement via automated OTIF tracking, targeting £4.3M saving through reduced expediting and performance credit recovery. (4) MAPE improvement — from 18.4% to below 12% across top-200 SKUs. (5) Total 3-year NPV at 12% WACC: £29.4M net of the £4.8M programme investment. Phase 1 go-live is targeted for Q3 2024 and will deliver KPIs 2 and 3 in the first year.

How should we approach dual-sourcing strategy for our Tier 1 critical suppliers?

Our dual-sourcing strategy for Tier 1 critical suppliers follows a risk-tiered qualification framework. For Category A suppliers (single-source, >15% production exposure) — SemiCore, Nexus Plastics, FlexSeal GmbH — we have initiated formal dual-source programmes with 6–18 month qualification timelines depending on technical complexity. The principle is that no Category A supplier should remain single-source beyond 24 months from programme inception. For SemiCore specifically, the qualification with Kyocera includes a full technical transfer of substrate specifications, 6-month parallel running, and independent quality audit. Safety stock policy has been simultaneously amended to 12-week cover for Category A during the qualification window, protecting production. The dual-sourcing programme has a budget of £2.1M for qualification activities (FMEA updates, tooling, audits) approved in the Q1 2024 capital plan.
